section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section provides the header and date for the maamar.
section.t: B"Sd.
Shabbos Parshas Mishpatim,
Mevarchim HaChodesh Adar Rishon 5741*

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section raises questions about the verse "And these are the judgments," noting the grammatical shift from plural to singular and the Jerusalem Talmud's interpretation of "tasim" as hidden treasure, and asks why the section begins with a Hebrew slave.
section.t: "And these are the judgments which you shall place before them: When you acquire a Hebrew slave, etc."¹
And the precise point in this is known,²
that "before them" is plural and third person, while "you shall acquire" is singular and second person.
Also, one must understand what is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud³
on the verse "And these are the judgments which you shall place before them,"
that "you shall place" is from the term "simah"
(a treasure)
that is not revealed, etc.,
the secrets of the Torah.
And it needs to be understood,
behold, judgments are the laws that are also understood by human intellect⁴
[and even by the intellect of the nations of the world⁵],
and what is the connection of judgments to "tasim" from the term "simah,"
the secrets of the Torah?
Also, one must understand⁶
why the judgments begin with the law of a Hebrew slave.⁷

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the Hebrew slave spiritually represents serving G-d with acceptance of the yoke, and that even intellectually understood commandments must be fulfilled with this submissive service, as the primary essence of all commandments is G-d's super-rational will.
section.t: Now, it is explained in Ohr HaTorah⁸
that the concept of a Hebrew slave in spirituality is
that his service of G-d is in the manner of acceptance of the yoke,
the service of a slave.
And based on this, it can be said,
that the fact that the judgments begin with the law of a Hebrew slave
is to hint
that even the fulfillment of the commandments of judgments,
which are understood by the intellect,
must be fulfilled from the aspect of acceptance of the yoke,
in the manner of the service of a slave.⁹

For although from the fact that these commandments are called in the Torah of Truth by the name "judgments," it is understood that these commandments must also be fulfilled from the aspect of reason,¹⁰
nevertheless,
the primary aspect of their fulfillment must be in the manner of acceptance of the yoke,
both from the perspective of the person fulfilling the commandments,
that his fulfillment of the commandments must be in the manner of the service of a slave,¹¹
and also from the perspective of the commandments,
for all the commandments
(even the commandments of judgments)
their essence is that they are the will of the Holy One, blessed be He,
a will that is above reason,
except that the Holy One, blessed be He, decreed that the will of these commandments should also be clothed in reason.¹²
And to add,
that this—that even the fulfillment of the commandments of judgments must be in the manner of acceptance of the yoke—
is also in the matter of the judgments within them.

That is, that these commandments must also be fulfilled from the aspect of reason is because such is the command of the Holy One, blessed be He, that the fulfillment of these commandments should also be from the aspect of reason.¹³
And it can be said,
that this is what our sages, of blessed memory, said¹⁴
on the verse "And these are the judgments,"
"And these" adds to the first ones; just as the first ones were from Sinai, so too these are from Sinai,
for at the giving of the Torah
(Sinai)
the Jewish people became slaves to the Holy One, blessed be He,¹⁵
and the hint of "even these are from Sinai" is,
that even the fulfillment of the commandments of judgments,
including also this matter that they must be fulfilled also from the aspect of reason
[even these,
judgments],
must be in the manner of the service of a slave.
And therefore the judgments begin with the law of a Hebrew slave,
in order to hint
that even the commandments of judgments,
the first approach
(the first approach)
to their study and fulfillment is acceptance of the yoke,
the service of a slave.¹⁶
And a further explanation,
that since the primary concept of slavery is with a Canaanite slave
[for in addition to the fact that a Hebrew slave serves only six years¹⁷
(and also a slave whose ear is pierced goes out in the Jubilee year¹⁸)
and regarding a Canaanite slave it is written,¹⁹
"Forever you shall work with them,"
the subjugation
(the slavery)
of a Hebrew slave
(even when he is a slave)
is not like the subjugation
(slavery)
of a Canaanite slave²⁰],
behold, in order to hint at the aforementioned concept
(that the fulfillment of the commandments of judgments must be in the manner of the service of a slave)
it would seemingly have been necessary for the judgments to begin with the law of a Canaanite slave.
